title: Prompt Engineering for Responsible Generative AI Use in African Education: A Report from a Three-Day Training Series
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of structured guidance for responsible prompt engineering in education, especially in African and other resource-constrained contexts where educators and researchers are beginning to use generative AI tools but often without strong ethical, pedagogical, or institutional support. The report examines how a short professional development programme can build prompt literacy and responsible AI use for teaching, academic writing, and research.

The intervention was a three-day online webinar training series organized by GenAI-ERA and delivered from July 3 to July 5, 2025. The sessions were scaffolded progressively from prompt foundations, to effective prompting, to advanced strategies such as zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and persona-guided prompting. Data came from a registration survey of 468 participants, webinar interaction records, facilitator observations, and session transcripts. The analysis combined descriptive statistics with qualitative and computational text-analysis techniques, including thematic indicators, reflexivity markers, and sentiment analysis.

Participants were drawn from multiple African countries and included tertiary/university educators, primary/secondary educators, postgraduate students, undergraduate students, researchers, and AI practitioners. In the education-focused taxonomy requested here, the relevant populations are undergraduate students, graduate/postgraduate students, and adult non-academic participants such as educators and researchers. The training context was fully online and centered largely on higher education and research use, though the report also discusses implications across broader educational levels.

The paper concludes that participants increasingly came to view prompt engineering as a form of AI literacy requiring ethical awareness, contextual sensitivity, and pedagogical judgment rather than mere technical skill. The report highlights strong demand for practical AI use in research and teaching, but also identifies persistent barriers including limited access to affordable tools, uneven prior experience, lack of locally relevant materials, and insufficient institutional guidance. It recommends sustained professional development, stronger ethical training, and formal integration of prompt literacy into curricula and inclusive AI initiatives across African education systems.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative AI tools used for text generation, prompting, academic writing, teaching support, and research assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluates a three-day professional development training series on responsible prompt engineering and ethical use of generative AI tools by educators, postgraduate students, and researchers in African higher education contexts.

findings.finding_summary: Across a three-day online training series with 468 participants, descriptive and transcript-based analyses indicated that participants increasingly recognised prompt engineering as a form of AI literacy requiring ethical awareness, contextual sensitivity, and pedagogical judgement. The report presents this as practical evidence that structured, scaffolded prompt-engineering training can support responsible GenAI use, but it does not report pre/post learning gains or causal effect sizes.
findings.measure: Participant discourse, webinar interaction records, facilitator observations, and transcript-based progressive learning/reflexivity/thematic/sentiment indicators

findings.finding_summary: Session analyses showed predominantly positive and neutral sentiment toward AI-related professional learning, with Session 3 reporting 84% neutral, 13.6% positive, and 2.4% negative sentiment in transcript segments. The authors interpret this as evidence of constructive engagement, growing confidence, and readiness to use advanced prompting strategies, though these are descriptive indicators rather than validated outcome measures.
findings.measure: VADER sentiment analysis of webinar transcripts

findings.finding_summary: The case report identified persistent implementation needs in low-resource African contexts, including access to affordable AI tools, locally relevant training materials, and sustained institutional support. These findings suggest training relevance and demand were high, but system-level constraints remained unresolved.
findings.measure: Registration survey responses, facilitator observations, webinar interactions, and transcript themes regarding access and institutional support

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive programme evaluation case report using surveys, webinar interactions, observations, and transcript analytics. It does not provide a controlled design or causal evidence of effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports encouraging descriptive signs of improved AI literacy engagement and positive sentiment, but no effect sizes, validated pre/post outcomes, or causal estimates are reported, so impact remains unclear.
